title: Press freedom around the world
subtitle: A right under pressure
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: Fewer than **10% of the world's people** live in a country with a truly free press. Between state censorship and economic pressure, this essential right is retreating almost everywhere.

hero.hook: Reporting the news can cost you your freedom, or your life: a journey into a fragile right.

blocks.text: **Press freedom** is one of the best indicators of a country's democratic health. It is not only the right to publish: it includes the ability of citizens to reach information that has been checked and is independent of those in power. Around the world, the right faces pressure from two sides: direct repression in authoritarian regimes, and a quieter erosion inside democracies themselves.

sections.title: A job that keeps getting more dangerous

blocks.text: Every year the organization [[Reporters Without Borders (RSF)]] publishes a benchmark report on the obstacles journalists face around the world.

blocks.caption: Fewer than 10% of the world's people live in a country with a truly free press

blocks.text: The 2024 data is alarming: fewer than **10%** of the world's people live where the press can work without hindrance. Countries like Norway keep high standards, but vast regions such as China, Russia and Iran treat investigative journalism as a form of treason.
In Turkmenistan, the state controls information so tightly that it banned the word “coronavirus” from the media at the start of the 2020 pandemic.
In 2023, at least 79 journalists lost their lives doing their job, often targeted to silence an inconvenient investigation. Close to 600 journalists are held in prison each year around the world.

Contrary to a common belief, press freedom is not won forever in Western countries. There it goes through quieter changes, tied to [[media concentration]] and to the financial influence of a few large groups.

In Hungary, [[Viktor Orbán]] built an effective strategy: instead of banning opposition outlets, he encouraged their purchase by allies of the government, slowly turning the media landscape into an official echo chamber.

In France, the debate is mostly about a handful of big groups owning the media, which raises the fear that newsrooms will censor themselves. Elsewhere, abusive lawsuits known as [[SLAPP]] are multiplying to intimidate critical voices.

sections.title: Money, the new adversary of journalism

blocks.text: Beyond political threats, journalism faces a deep economic crisis. The old model, built on single-copy sales and advertising, collapsed with the digital shift, as the big platforms captured most online advertising.

blocks.caption: The historic business model of the press collapsed with the digital shift

blocks.text: That loss of revenue is closing local papers and creating “news deserts” where nobody watches what elected officials do. New models are emerging in response, funded by donations or direct subscriptions, like Mediapart in France and ProPublica in the United States, which prove that independent journalism can also pay for itself.
The first printed newspaper in history, the “Relation,” was launched in Strasbourg in 1605 by Johann Carolus, long before press freedom existed in law.

sections.title: Checking reality in a world flooded with images

blocks.text: The digital age made information faster, but it also opened the door to [[disinformation]]. Social media algorithms favor emotional content over factual analysis, breaking up our shared picture of the world.

So the journalist's role is shifting toward that of a “verifier” of reality, inside a permanent flow of images and data. The ethical questions get harder, as in photojournalism in a war zone, where respect for human dignity sometimes collides with the need to show what happened.

Defending press freedom therefore means better regulation of the big digital platforms and stronger media education. Without a free press able to check the facts, democratic debate risks dissolving into a world where every opinion counts the same, however untrue.

Fewer than 10% of the world's people live in a country with a truly free press. Between direct repression, economic pressure and digital disinformation, a right that democracy depends on is retreating almost everywhere.
